title: Using Methylation Clocks to Evaluate Anti-Aging Interventions | Aging
abstract: # Using Methylation Clocks to Evaluate Anti-Aging Interventions. The methylation profile of a smoker is useful in constructing a GrimAge clock, but it should be counted in reverse for the purpose of evaluating anti-aging interventions. In fact, methylation changes associated with smoking were included in the GrimAge clock with positive coefficients simply because they’re statistically associated with a shorter life expectancy. All type two changes should be counted with negative coefficients in methylation clocks, even though they’re statistically associated with older ages and shorter remaining lifespan. Our methylation clock should be calibrated to be sure that the changes associated with CR are scored toward a younger biological age. For my Aging US publication, I created a methylation clock that is truly based on stochastic changes only. So in summary, methylation clocks to date have been of limited utility for the purpose of evaluating anti-aging interventions because they mix detrimental and beneficial epigenetic changes that take place with age, which I call type one and type respectively.
